text: Dana states the numbers plainly: Harrow Peak Outfitters can tolerate up to 4 hours of downtime before it's a real problem, and can afford to lose at most 1 hour of order data if something has to be restored from a backup. Those are business decisions, and Chapter 5 is clear they drive the backup design, not the other way around -- so each resource ends up with a policy that actually fits what it holds, instead of one generic schedule applied everywhere.

The database's continuous log backups give point-in-time restore within minutes, comfortably inside the 1-hour RPO. The app VM holds mostly stateless configuration, so a daily backup is enough for it. The storage account gets soft delete, versioning, and geo-redundant storage, protecting invoices and images against both accidental deletion and a regional outage.

A backup job reporting success every night proves nothing about whether a restore actually works, so three get tested for real: a deleted test invoice recovered from soft delete, a point-in-time restore of the database to a scratch copy with the test order row confirmed intact, and the app VM restored from a recovery point and confirmed to boot clean. All three pass before the policy counts as done.

During final testing, a blob upload fails with a 403 -- right when everything was supposed to be finished. Checking connectivity first rules out a network-down problem; checking the RBAC role assignment rules out a missing permission. The actual cause is one layer deeper: the storage account's firewall allows only selected virtual networks, and app-subnet was never added to that list. Adding it fixes the error, and the retest comes back clean.

With the restore tests passed and the real bug fixed, documentation gets written for whoever inherits this environment next: an as-built diagram, a runbook, and a handoff checklist that names two deferred items honestly instead of hiding them. Next: reviewing the whole seven-course arc this capstone closes out, and what it makes you ready for.
